setter.evidence: No KFS/KL/DH suffix in the title and no setter is named on the call. The lead is inbound from an ad: "what did I see that the ad was for, hey, there's, we're taking a select number of, I can't remember what it was", plus a prior download of Trevor's Guide.

prospect.name: Andy
prospect.location: New Zealand (small town); originally from the USA
prospect.occupation: Self-employed event director — puts on his own expedition-length adventure race (one intense month a year, flexible the rest); previously a river-trip guide; recently started a new job
prospect.family_status: Going through a separation after a 25-year marriage, on good terms ('I'm really good friends with the woman I'm separating from'); two sons, one 17 and at university studying sports science; has a twin brother who is a professional adventure racer
prospect.training_background: Lifelong athlete. Expedition climbing when younger, then surfing and paddling, then endurance sport (Ironman-type racing), now expedition-level adventure racing (seven- and eight-day events; next one in India, at altitude). Wrote a book on using high-intensity interval training for endurance; physics degree. Currently trains roughly 8-10 sessions a week: 1-2 kettlebell days, 2 traditional lifting days, ~3 cycling days on a smart trainer, climbing 3-4 nights a week, plus three-minute bar hangs 4-5x/week and loaded carries (farmer, suitcase, racked, on a treadmill).
prospect.medical: Bilateral hip replacements — first about four to five years ago, second roughly 18 months later, clear of surgery about two to two and a half years. Cause described as a congenital condition ('not a genetic deformity, but I have a condition') compounded by extreme endurance volume; his twin brother needed the same. Residual limitation: 'the hip socket has changed because it's artificial now. So I don't have as much surface and it can pop out more easily, and that's bad.' Also arthritic shoulders and sore elbows from heavy lifting and weighted pull-ups, and a prior back injury from deadlifting that required four weeks of physio.

signals: Self-directed and highly capable: physics degree, wrote a book on endurance training, has taught himself most of the basic kettlebell movements from free content — 'I've taught myself most of the basic moves.'

Anchored to a cheap alternative that genuinely worked, and the alternative is Primal's own free content: 'one of the things I started doing of Trevor's that I really liked was the halo workout, he calls it 28s... made my shoulders better, and so I'm now surfing again, and without as much pain.'

Volunteered an explicit anti-premium-programme thesis: 'really it all works... what it takes is consistency... it's not like the kettlebell's a magical tool... all the other stuff is, to some extent, what flavor you want to use to get there.'
Has free expert coaching already: a twin brother who races professionally is programming his endurance block, and his sports-science-student son advises on nutrition.

COUNTER-SIGNAL toward the_optimizer: he is genuinely fit with nothing wrong ('there's nothing wrong right now'), wants good-to-great, and did not devalue the offer ('I'm not devaluing it at all'). The reason the_optimizer was not assigned is that for the_optimizer price is a quality signal rather than a barrier, and here price was the binding constraint — 'that's a substantial portion of my annual income.'

goals.text: Learn how to progress properly with kettlebells — load selection, programming and progression — instead of guessing
Progress without hurting himself; he currently picks weights that are too heavy for complexes and is wrecked the next day
Improve mobility, which he names as his single biggest weakness, around two artificial hips
Be able to train anywhere — from his van on surf trips and road trips — with a couple of kettlebells, instead of scheduling work around gym days
Stay strong and capable enough to keep climbing, surfing and adventure racing rather than becoming 'a cyclist that doesn't have any muscle'
Shift the balance of his training toward kettlebells because they are kinder to his joints than traditional lifting
Keep muscle and like how he looks, without chasing a sculpted physique
Reconnect with who he was and what he loves doing, after subordinating those things during a 25-year marriage that is now ending
Possibly become a trainer as a side business in his small town, using kettlebell knowledge as the credential
Be prepared for an expedition adventure race in India at altitude — but he explicitly parks this outside the programme, as his twin brother is already coaching him for it

pains.text: Joint damage from traditional lifting — arthritic shoulders and elbows that ache the morning after heavy work and weighted pull-ups: 'I wake up in the morning and I'm like, why am I so sore?'
Two hip replacements leave less socket surface, so the joint 'can pop out more easily' on some movements and he has to be careful with load and range
Does not know kettlebell progression, so he over-loads complexes and is excessively sore: 'sometimes I'll do complexes, and I choose way too heavy, and then I'm really sore the next day'

Too much conflicting kettlebell material online; self-programming would cost him a lot of time: 'there's so much stuff out there, I could spend a lot of time creating my own program, and then trying to optimize that'
Training is tethered to a gym, so he now fits work — course-setting for the races he runs — around his gym days: 'now I'm trying to fit it around my gym days, which is silly'

A hard emotional stretch around the separation; the gym has become his coping mechanism: 'it's been a bit of a coping mechanism, a positive one... it's kept me grounded. I've had a couple of tricky years.'
Earlier hip decline cost him work and his mood — he had to stop guiding and 'started just getting depressed because I couldn't go on run'; two years of failed conservative attempts before surgery

objections.raw_quote: There is a financial concern for me at the moment. I'm very time-free and my kids are out the house, which is good, but that is a significant, that would be a significant investment for me. So I'd have to think about ways to make that, yeah, make that, make that work.
objections.rep_response: Ran the isolation move correctly — 'So apart from finances, like, sounds good to you, like there's nothing else?' — got a clean yes on everything except money, and then stopped. No payment plan was floated, no permission was asked for an open financial conversation, and none of the financial-picture questions (cash on hand, monthly surplus, credit cards, available credit, investments) were asked. The rep pivoted straight to scheduling a follow-up.

objections.raw_quote: Well, I have to figure out if I can run it through my business, for one. That's my first step.
objections.rep_response: Asked a good clarifying question — 'When you say run it through your business, what do you mean exactly?' — and let Andy explain the New Zealand tax treatment, then asked for a timeline on getting an answer from the accountant. The rep did not help him build the professional-development case, offer an invoice or receipt framing, or explore whether the coaching-business angle would strengthen the deductibility argument.

objections.raw_quote: that's really looking at about 7,500 New Zealand dollars for me because of the exchange rate. So we're, if I still had money, because I'm from the U.S. originally, so if I still had my U.S. money, would be a lot different.
objections.rep_response: No response at all. The rep did not acknowledge the currency conversion or reframe the number, and moved directly to booking Friday.

objections.raw_quote: So I will, let me think, and I can have some time to think about that, right?
objections.rep_response: Granted it immediately — 'Let me know what are your thoughts on that, so we can...' — and booked a call for Friday at 6.30pm New Zealand time. None of the Objection A moves were run: no 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you there', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in'.

evidence: No payment, no verbal agreement, no payment link. Andy asked for time: 'let me think, and I can have some time to think about that, right?'

A concrete next call was set and confirmed: 'So how about on Friday if we schedule a call at 6.30 p.m., your time?' ... 'Okay, so 6.30pm, Friday, 29. Okay, so I will set up a meeting and you'll get the invite through your email.' Andy confirmed: 'Cool. Perfect.'

Two real, named blockers remain open: an accountant's answer on whether the fee is deductible as professional development in New Zealand, and whether he wants to spend what he calls a substantial portion of his annual income.

Positive signal — full needs agreement on everything but money: 'apart from the finances, the three months of, yeah, three months is good. Everything else, the way that it works and what I think I would get out of it are good.'

Counter-evidence against optimism: he twice framed the price as larger than expected ('probably I had thought that it would be quite that expensive'), converted it to ~NZ$7,500, and called it a substantial portion of annual income. The financial constraint is real, not a stall, and it was never worked.
outcome.next_step: Follow-up call booked for Friday 29 May, 6.30pm New Zealand time; rep to send the calendar invite by email. Andy to email his accountant this week about expensing the programme through his business as professional development, and to decide whether he wants to make the investment.

notable.note: Four things a manager should look at. (1) PRICING DEVIATION: the rep quoted a three-month tier at $4,000 USD. The documented offer is $6,000 / 6 months and $9,000 / 12 months; a three-month tier does not exist in it. He also volunteered 'we have like three tiers' and 'most of the guys go for the 12-month and six-month.' Someone needs to confirm whether a $4,000 / 3-month product is sanctioned. (2) PROACTIVE DOWN-SELL: the rep talked the prospect off the standard tiers unprompted and before any price was on the table — 'Most of the guys go for the 12-month and six-month, but that's not for you, in my opinion, because you're already in kettlebells... My advice would be go with the three-month program.' He then still lost the deal on price, so the discount bought nothing. (3) FRAME INVERSION: at 00:09:07 the rep disclosed that he personally needs a hip replacement and asked the prospect for advice — 'Would you advise someone to go for it? Because I have to do it too... That's me. I'm waiting at least five, 15 years.' The prospect then coached the rep for roughly three minutes. Discovery never recovered its authority after this. (4) The prospect's two artificial hips, with a stated dislocation risk, were never addressed in the training-and-mobility pillar despite being the one clinical fact that governs whether he can do the programme — the same clinical blind spot already logged as a known gap in the script. Also: the prospect's name is 'Andy' only; no surname was ever given, and the file title contains the rep's name plus a Polish Zoom string rather than the prospect's.

quality.notes: Extensive and sustained inversion; roles were resolved from content throughout. Whole passages sit under the wrong label — for example the block at 00:02:34 attributed to 'Andrew Jin (Primal Instinct)' ('I have two sons and they started getting into that age, like 14, 15... so I rejoined the gym with them') is unmistakably Andy, and the entire pillar presentation from roughly 00:35:31 to 00:39:32 ('Trevor probably could mainly fine-tune it', 'third piece, the accountability', 'you get his phone number') is attributed to Andy but is unmistakably the rep. The pricing exchange around 00:42:00-00:43:08 alternates incorrectly, with 'My advice would be go with the three-month program' landing under Andy's label and 'that sounds about the right amount of time' landing under the rep's. Prospect connection quality was also poor — he joined from a phone, dropped and froze several times, and the rep asked him to return to a room. Separately, the rep's display label reads 'Andrew Jin (Primal Instinct)' while the file title, the Drive folder and the stated location (Poland) all point to Andrew Musial; recorded as Andrew Musial, flagged for a human to confirm the two names are the same person.
